fable

/FAY-buhl/ - the stress falls on FAY · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A fable is a short, openly invented tale that teaches a lesson — often through talking animals — and, by extension, any account that is invention rather than fact.

Grandfather passed it off as family history, but the tale of the wolf who guarded our orchard is pure fable — no wolf, no orchard, just a lesson about patience he wanted us to keep.

Example

In the sailors' fable, a gull trades her wings to a fish for a coat of silver scales — and spends the rest of the tale sinking slowly, wishing back what she gave away.

No one who tells it thinks a gull ever made such a bargain, and that is the point. A fable does not ask to be believed: it is invention worn openly, animals doing impossible things so that the lesson underneath — what you surrender to become what you envy — can be handed over without an argument.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

parable: A parable teaches through lifelike, everyday people — two debtors, a lost sheep, a quarrel over a well — events that could happen on any street. A fable announces its invention from the first line: talking beasts, impossible bargains, a tale nobody was ever meant to believe.

yarn: A yarn is a long, colorful story spun mainly for the fun of the telling, and it sprawls wherever the teller wanders. A fable is compact and aimed: every invented detail exists to deliver the one lesson waiting at the end.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

chronicle: a plain, dated record of what actually happened

eyewitness account: testimony bound to what was really seen

Where it sits · how much of the world the story takes on

anecdote → fable → myth

anecdote vs. fable: An anecdote is milder stuff than a fable: one small moment offered as true, nothing invented and nothing to prove — a fable invents freely and aims its whole tale at a single lesson.

myth vs. fable: Myth goes further than fable: a fable spends its invention on one compact lesson, while a myth swells to carry a people's entire picture of the world — origins, gods, and all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — fab: speak, tell (Latin fari, whose noun fabula meant 'the thing told')

Suffix — -le: noun ending, worn down from Latin -ula

Put it together: Latin fari, to speak, grew the noun fabula — 'the thing told' — and French wore it down to fable. At root, a fable is simply a telling: a story that lives in the mouth before it lives anywhere else. The same speaking root murmurs inside affable, ineffable, and even infant.

Use the root in a new word: affable: Fans lingered at the affable shortstop's locker long after the loss, and even the beat writers went home smiling.

Root Check

Word Choice

literary / storytelling

Fable is a genre label first — Aesop's talking foxes — but English also uses it dismissively, for any account that is invention wearing the clothes of fact: 'the numbers in the prospectus were pure fable.' Its neighbors divide the storytelling work: a parable keeps to lifelike, everyday people; a legend attaches itself to a real name or place and grows in the telling; a myth expands to explain a people's whole world. In this unit's spirit, remember the dismissive sense — calling a report a fable is a polite way of calling it false.
